name: Metabolife

lead: Metabolife 356 was a top-selling diet supplement combining ephedra and caffeine, sold from the mid-1990s by Metabolife International. Dieters used it for more energy, less appetite and faster weight loss for a leaner look.

Ephedra's alkaloids and caffeine stimulate the sympathetic nervous system, raising heart rate and metabolic rate and suppressing appetite. The ephedra-caffeine combination has been studied for short-term weight loss. It is documented here as a historical example.

paras: It was sold through a customer-driven distribution model and used during diets for energy and appetite control. It is no longer available in its ephedra form after the 2004 US ban.

A 2004 randomized trial found cardiovascular effects, and case reports describe heart attack, stroke, psychosis and diabetic ketoacidosis. Ephedra supplements have been banned in the US since 2004, and the company filed for bankruptcy in 2005 after adverse-event reports, a congressional investigation and litigation.

angle.text: Metabolife 356 was the best-selling fat burner of its era, taken by dieters for energy and appetite control on the way to a leaner look. Its ephedra-caffeine combination has been studied for short-term weight loss; it is documented here as a historical example after the federal ephedra ban.

lead: Metabolife was a San Diego company founded in the 1990s by Michael Ellis, best known for Metabolife 356, an ephedra- and caffeine-based weight-loss and energy supplement sold largely through a customer-driven distribution model [1][2]. At its peak it was the top-selling dietary weight-loss supplement in the United States [3].

Ephedra raises heart rate and blood pressure, and the product was the subject of adverse-event reports, a randomized trial that found cardiovascular effects, a congressional investigation, litigation and, in 2004, a US ban on ephedra-containing supplements [2][3]. The company filed for bankruptcy in 2005 and its non-ephedra assets were later sold [2].

paras: Accounts differ on dates. Grokipedia says the company was founded in 1995 and that the formula was developed in 1989 [1]; Wikipedia places the founding in the early 1990s, with Metabolife 356 initially marketed to bodybuilders in 1995 before rebranding as a diet aid [2]. David Brown succeeded Ellis as chief executive in September 2000 [1][2].

A House committee investigation in October 2002 reported thousands of serious adverse-event reports and criticized the company's handling of them [2]. Ellis was indicted in 2004 for false statements to the FDA and pleaded guilty to one count, receiving a six-month prison sentence [1][2]. The company sought bankruptcy protection in July 2005 amid litigation, and Ideasphere bought the non-ephedra assets in 2007 [2].

A randomized controlled trial published in JAMA in 2004 tested Metabolife 356 for effects on QTc interval and systolic blood pressure, prompted by reports of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events [3]. Wikipedia summarizes it as finding raised blood pressure and mild arrhythmias [2]. A separate Holter-monitoring study in healthy volunteers also examined the product [4].

Case reports describe a myocardial infarction after years of Metabolife 356 use [5], ischemic strokes after ephedra products including Metabolife 356 [6], psychosis and delirium [7], and diabetic ketoacidosis in two cases [8]. A 2006 analysis examined metal content in ephedra supplements [9]. A later study tested an ephedra-free multicomponent supplement for ECG effects in volunteers [10].

Human trials examined cardiovascular safety rather than weight loss. The 2004 JAMA randomized trial measured ECG and blood-pressure outcomes of the ephedra-and-caffeine product [3], and a 2003 study used Holter monitoring and hemostatic parameters in healthy volunteers [4]. Grokipedia states that randomized trials of ephedra itself supported short-term weight reduction, but that hazards were dose-dependent [1].
